title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation of operator intent into device configuration promises faster NetOps workflows but creates operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or unsafe. Recent architectural proposals therefore advocate a generate→verify→repair pattern that pairs probabilistic LLM generators with deterministic validators and bounded repair adapters as floor‑safety nets. However, there is limited preregistered, paired A/B evidence quantifying how narrowly bounded guarded pipelines affect first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics.

This work implements a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment that evaluates a minimal guarded pipeline composed of: (1) a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), (2) a frozen deterministic validator performing rule and dependency checks and canonicalization, and (3) at most one automated repair attempt when the validator detects violations. The central research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Our contributions are: (i) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and full archival of model outputs and validator/repair traces; (ii) confirmatory statistics computed from the archived artifacts showing a near‑ceiling baseline and a single corrected discordance; (iii) a compact post‑hoc sensitivity quantification tied directly to observed contingency counts; and (iv) artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and system papers document the promise and risk of using LLMs for network configuration: LLMs can synthesize templates and translate intent into device commands in controlled settings, yet they exhibit failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313; 10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Work in other domains demonstrates that verifier‑assisted pipelines, retrieval augmentation, and bounded repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating similar mitigations for NetOps pipelines [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1; 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Classic deterministic verification algorithms (e.g., header‑space analysis and specification‑based checking) provide algorithmic foundations for validators that statically check reachability, ordering, and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834].

Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these strands: it measures, under preregistered paired semantics, whether a frozen deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration meaningfully changes first‑pass validity counts on a controlled synthetic task bank. Unlike broader benchmarks that compare model knowledge, our design focuses on the operational reliability of a guarded generate→verify→repair architectural pattern.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The experiment was preregistered prior to observing outcomes (id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1). Confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly used a planning assumption of planned baseline pass rate = 0.40 to compute power and motivate the N=300 paired tasks.

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds from a frozen task generator. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate was reused in both arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics): baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (same candidate validated and—if invalid—subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The preregistered choice to share the initial candidate isolates the validator/repair intervention’s effect on a single generated plan but increases within‑pair correlation and reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available for McNemar inference compared with independent‑draws designs.

Model, validator, and scoring: The declared model was gpt-5-mini. A frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements rule and dependency checks, canonicalizes outputs to normalized ASTs, and emits binary pass/fail scoring plus violation codes used to trigger and steer the automated repair. The scoring rule used in the confirmatory analysis required the validator to confirm that the generated configuration satisfied all preregistered intent constraints and required command sequences; only such validated outputs were scored as successes.

Missingness, retries, and planned analysis: The preregistration allowed a single retry for provider infra failures. The execution followed the pre-specified missingness plan: primary analysis 'complete_pair_primary' drops only pairs where both calls fail; sensitivity analyses treat failed calls as failures. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test (α=0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes; we also computed the absolute risk difference and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap seed = 1729). Secondary analyses included exact binomial intervals for repair success and sensitivity checks for missingness and contamination. All analysis code and per‑task artifacts are archived in the run’s evidence bundle and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement.

Design rationale and tradeoffs: The single‑iteration repair budget and shared candidate semantics reflect a conservative operational floor‑guardrail: evaluate whether a minimal automated remediation can correct validator‑detected violations on a single proposed plan. These choices reduce cross‑arm variability and represent an operationally plausible workflow (produce one plan, then attempt bounded automated repair before human review). They also reduce the number of discordant pairs informative for McNemar inference; we discuss the inferential consequences in Results.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run executed the preregistered workload and completed all planned episodes: planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used totaled 301; the repair stage was invoked exactly once. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; there were zero failed episodes and no deterministic exclusions for contamination under the preregistered checks.

Primary outcomes (artifact counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). The paired contingency (guarded vs baseline) observed in the archived analysis artifact is: n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). These contingency counts were extracted directly from the archived paired contingency artifact and form the basis of confirmatory inference.

Confirmatory inference (preregistered): Applying the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test to the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. The observed absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline success rate) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference is [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); the Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for 1/1 is [0.025, 1.0], indicating wide uncertainty due to the single observed repair case.

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound from observed contingency: The total number of discordant pairs observed is n10 + n01 = 1. Under the run’s paired sampling semantics, this discordant‑pair total imposes a hard limit on achievable absolute paired differences equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. In practical terms: (a) with the observed discordant count, the maximal resolvable absolute improvement is 1/300; (b) the preregistered planning target (≥50% relative reduction given planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) corresponds to an absolute improvement of roughly 0.30 (≈90/300 discordant pairs in favor of guarded) and therefore could not have been detected given the realized baseline prevalence. This artifact‑grounded sensitivity bound explains why the preregistered primary hypothesis (H1) lacks empirical support despite the guarded arm achieving 100% validity.

Representative diagnostic traces: For each episode the validator trace archived normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and repair_applied flags. The single baseline failure’s trace shows a validator‑detected violation that the preregistered repair adapter remediated on its single permitted invocation; the post‑repair normalized_configuration satisfied the full intent constraints. The execution manifest and analysis artifacts contain the per‑task validator decisions and repair trace for inspection; these artifacts are enumerated in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational consequences: The guarded pipeline corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, demonstrating that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can remediate validator‑detected violations in specific cases. However, because the empirical baseline pass rate (299/300) was far higher than the preregistered planning assumption (0.40), the experiment had essentially no statistical headroom to detect the large relative effect preregistered under H1.

Implications for preregistration and power planning: Confirmatory NetOps experiments that rely on paired McNemar inference must account explicitly for the expected number of informative discordant pairs, not only overall N. When baseline pass rate uncertainty is high, preregistration should either (i) specify an expected initial‑failure count (and target discordant pairs), (ii) calibrate the task bank difficulty to induce the desired failure prevalence, or (iii) change the primary estimand to a conditional probability (e.g., repair success conditional on initial failure) and power the study accordingly. In our run, the preregistered planning assumption (baseline = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed data, a fact we declare and quantify here using artifact counts.

Pairing semantics and experimental realism: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate design isolates the validator/repair effect on a single generated plan but reduces cross‑arm independence and therefore the number of discordant pairs. Independent generation per arm would increase discordant pairs and statistical information but mixes generator variability into the estimand. Choice of pairing semantics should therefore match the operational claim: if the claim concerns remediating a fixed generated plan, shared‑candidate pairing is appropriate; if the claim concerns overall end‑to‑end improvements when the model can re‑sample, independent draws per arm may be preferable.

Construct and external validity limits: The deterministic validator checks canonicalized configuration constraints rather than executing configurations in a live network; packet‑level reachability and performance effects were not measured. The task bank was synthetic and constrained to a small set of vendor template variants; the model family was a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation was used. These design choices limit generality to production environments with heterogeneous vendors and runtime dynamics. The manuscript enumerates these limitations explicitly and attaches artifact‑grounded evidence to each claim.

Recommendations for future confirmatory evaluations: (1) preregister and calibrate task banks to produce a targeted initial‑failure prevalence (or a target number of informative discordant pairs) matched to the planned effect size; (2) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets and include their impact on expected discordant pairs in power planning; (3) when operational claims require runtime assurances, integrate emulation or controlled execution steps to measure packet‑ and control‑plane consequences rather than relying solely on static validators; (4) when repair effectiveness is primary, treat it as a conditional estimand (conditional on initial failure) and ensure the run is powered for sufficient initial failures to estimate that probability precisely.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) applying a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget to gpt-5-mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 valid outputs and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output. However, the run does not support the preregistered large relative effect (≥50% reduction in misconfiguration) because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) and produced effectively no statistical headroom. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should calibrate task difficulty to achieve informative discordant counts, align pairing semantics with operational claims, and incorporate emulation when runtime effects are relevant. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit verification of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs informative for McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; a larger sample of initial failures is required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
